title: Detecting Complications Early
html:
Reduction of risk potential focuses on preventing complications from treatments, procedures, diagnostics, and existing conditions. Strong nursing judgment recognizes a concerning pattern before a single value becomes catastrophic.

Trend, do not snapshot

  • Compare current findings with baseline, expected recovery, and earlier measurements.
  • Cluster vital signs, symptoms, intake and output, laboratory results, and procedure-specific checks.
  • Distinguish an expected effect from a finding that requires immediate intervention or escalation.
Validate without delaying rescue
Recheck a surprising value when error is plausible, but do not postpone urgent action when the client also shows clinical instability.

Protect before and after procedures

Confirm preparation requirements, allergies, relevant results, consent status, and baseline neurovascular or functional findings. After the procedure, monitor the specific complications most likely to cause early harm.

Communicate the pattern

Escalation is stronger when it states the change, trend, relevant background, current assessment, action already taken, and the response you need now.

Learning goals

Compare findings over time, connect a procedure to its likely complications, and communicate a time-critical concern without delaying assessment. This is an introduction to surveillance, not a substitute for system-specific assessment training.

Use a focused baseline

Before a procedure, identify what will be compared afterward: mental status, respiratory effort, circulation, pain, the procedure site, and relevant intake and output. Confirm preparation and consent requirements according to role and policy. If the client describes unanswered questions about risks, pause preparation and contact the procedural clinician; witnessing a signature does not replace informed discussion.

Look for clusters

A postoperative client with rising heart rate, falling blood pressure, pallor, and reduced urine output needs prompt evaluation for poor perfusion, including possible bleeding. Do not dismiss the pattern because one value is still within a reference range. Conversely, an unexpected result without symptoms may need careful verification. Assess the client while arranging verification; clinical instability cannot wait for a repeat result.

After a limb procedure or cast, compare pain, movement, sensation, skin temperature, and circulation with baseline and the other limb when appropriate. Worsening pain out of proportion, pain with passive movement, new numbness, or weakness warrants urgent review. A palpable pulse alone does not rule out compartment syndrome.

Make escalation actionable

Use SBAR with actual times and trends: “After the procedure, pulse rose from 88 to 118, blood pressure fell, and urine output decreased. The client is pale. I need an immediate bedside assessment.” Follow the chain of escalation if the response is inadequate. Continue surveillance and document who was contacted, the response, actions, and reassessment.

Evaluate, not just report

A callback is not an outcome. Reassess whether symptoms and perfusion improve after interventions, whether prescribed monitoring is feasible, and whether a higher level of care is needed. During handover, assign responsibility for pending tests and specify which changes require urgent action.
